ad4_wage_split.topic: Productivity–pay split since 1973/1979 and the measurement dispute

claims.text: EPI (updated 14 Sep 2026): from 1979 Q4 to 2026 Q2 total-economy net productivity rose 93.7% and the hourly compensation of production and nonsupervisory private-sector workers rose 32.7%; productivity 'has grown 2.9x as much as pay'.

EPI definitions: productivity = output less depreciation per hour, total economy; pay = average hourly compensation (wages plus benefits) of production/nonsupervisory private workers (~80% of private workforce); both deflated by the same spliced CPI series (CPI-U-RS 1978–99, chained CPI-U from 2000).

EPI attributes the gap to policy choices: tolerated excess unemployment, smaller and rarer minimum-wage increases, labor law that 'failed to keep pace', lower top tax rates, deregulation and weaker antitrust.

Feldstein (NBER w13953, 2008): 1970–2006 nonfarm business productivity rose 1.9%/yr and real compensation per hour 1.7%/yr when both are deflated by the same nonfarm business output price index; employee compensation was 66% of national income in 1970 and 64% in 2006; the two errors he identifies are using wages rather than total compensation and using different deflators.

BLS Beyond the Numbers (June 2017), 183 industries 1987–2015: productivity outpaced compensation in 83% of industries; in the median industry the output deflator grew about 0.6 point a year slower than the CPI and labor share fell about 0.6% a year — 'the median effect of the change in labor share was the same as that of the difference in deflators.'

Sherk (Heritage, 17 Jul 2013), 1973–2012: productivity +100%, hourly compensation +77% when measured consistently; attributes 35% of the apparent gap to using wages of a subset of workers instead of total compensation of all, 44% to different inflation measures, 21% to other factors (depreciation, import prices); calls most of the gap 'a statistical illusion'; acknowledges median pay grew more slowly than average productivity.

Strain (Aspen ESG 2019), citing Stansbury and Summers (2017), 1975–2015: a one-point rise in productivity growth is associated with 0.73 point higher compensation growth for the median worker, 0.74 for average compensation, 0.53 for production/nonsupervisory workers; non-wage compensation rose from about 14% to about 19% of pay; concedes real wage growth of ~0.5%/yr is not strong and gains are unequally distributed.

Strain summarises Lawrence (2016): using total economy and net output reduces the 2013 gap by 20%, using compensation by 8.2%, including managers/professionals explains 30%, deflating by an output price index explains 35%.

Real average hourly earnings peaked in January 1973 at $4.03, equal to $23.68 in 2018 dollars; wages and salaries are about 70% of compensation; since 2000 real usual weekly wages rose 3% for the lowest tenth and 15.7% for the top tenth.

ad4_labor_power.topic: Union density, PATCO, strikes, labor-law enforcement 1981–2026

claims.text: BLS union membership rates (wage and salary workers): all 20.1% (1983), 16.0% (1990), 13.4% (2000), 11.9% (2010), 11.1% (2015); private sector 16.8%, 12.0%, 9.0%, 6.9%, 6.7%; public sector 36.7%, 36.4%, 36.9%, 36.2%, 35.2%. Private-sector members fell from 11.93m (1983) to 7.55m (2015) while wage and salary employment rose from 88.3m to 133.7m.

PATCO members struck at 7 a.m. on 3 August 1981; Reagan gave them 48 hours to return; on 5 August more than 11,000 were fired; federal law (1978) prohibited federal employees from striking; the union was decertified in late 1981.

About 13,000 PATCO members walked out on 3 Aug 1981; Reagan fired the 11,345 who stayed out; PATCO decertified 22 Oct 1981; demands were higher pay, fewer hours, better retirement; a June 1981 tentative deal (up to 11% pay) was rejected by members; PATCO had endorsed Reagan over Carter in 1980.
NLRB v. Mackay Radio (16 May 1938): an employer 'is not bound to discharge those hired to fill the places of strikers' — permanent replacement of economic strikers lawful since 1938.

EPI (Dec 2019): at least one unfair-labor-practice charge was filed in 41.5% of NLRB-supervised elections in 2016–17 (a charge is an allegation, not a finding); illegal-firing charges in 19.9% (narrow) to 29.6% (broad); 54.4% in units over 60 workers; the NLRA has no civil penalties — fired workers get back pay minus interim earnings; employers spend an estimated nearly $340m a year on union-avoidance consultants.

Trump v. Slaughter (No. 25-332), decided 29 June 2026, 6–3, opinion by Roberts: for-cause removal protection for FTC commissioners unconstitutional, overruling Humphrey's Executor; Proskauer judges it 'highly likely' the NLRA's removal protection for Board members falls too; Wilcox's challenge to her early-2025 removal appears resolved by it.
NLRB quorum restored 7 Jan 2026 when James Murphy and Scott Mayer were sworn in; Crystal Carey sworn in as General Counsel the same day.

Senate confirmed James Macy (R, term to Aug 2030) and David Prouty (D, renominated, to Aug 2031) on 7 Aug 2026 in a 74-nominee en bloc package passed 51–47; Board has four members, 3–1 Republican majority, one vacancy.

Farber et al. (QJE 2021), using Gallup and other survey microdata from 1936: US income inequality has varied inversely with union density over 100 years; the household union premium held between 10 and 20 log points despite large changes in density; at the mid-century peak union households were less educated and more nonwhite than others; an instrumental-variable strategy finds 'unions reduce inequality'.

ad4_shareholder_turn.topic: Shareholder primacy, Rule 10b-18, buybacks, CEO pay, 1981/1986 tax laws, Volcker

claims.text: Friedman's essay ran in the New York Times Magazine on 13 Sep 1970; it states there is 'one and only one social responsibility of business' — to increase profits 'so long as it stays within the rules of the game' — and that 'a corporate executive is an employee of the owners of the business.'
Jensen and Meckling (Journal of Financial Economics 3(4), 1976) define agency costs arising from the separation of ownership and control and the costs generated by debt and outside equity.

SEC Rule 10b-18 was adopted in Exchange Act Release No. 19244 (17 Nov 1982), 47 FR 53333 (26 Nov 1982); it provides a safe harbor so that an issuer is not deemed to violate Sections 9(a)(2), 10(b) or Rule 10b-5 solely because of the manner, timing, price or volume of its repurchases if it meets four conditions: one broker per day, no purchases at the open or near the close, price no higher than the highest independent bid or last independent trade, and daily volume generally no more than 25% of average daily trading volume. Compliance is voluntary and there is no presumption that purchases outside it are manipulative; 2003 amendments updated it.

The SEC's 2023 Share Repurchase Disclosure Modernization rules (daily repurchase data, narrative on objectives) were vacated by the Fifth Circuit on 19 Dec 2023 after the SEC failed to cure defects identified on 31 Oct 2023.

S&P 500 buybacks (S&P DJI): 2018 $806.41bn; 2019 $728.74bn; 2020 $519.76bn; 2021 $881.72bn; 2022 $922.68bn; 2023 $795.16bn; 2024 $942.55bn (record); 12 months to Sep 2025 $1.020tn (record); Q3 2025 $249.0bn; top 20 companies 49.5% of Q3 2025 buybacks (historical average 47.8%); 17.1% of companies cut share count used for EPS by at least 4% year on year; dividends 12 months to Sep 2025 $664.9bn; 1% excise tax Q3 2025 $2.25bn (0.36% of operating earnings), 2023 $7.47bn; Silverblatt: 'The 1% tax continues to be a manageable expense and has not impacted overall buybacks.'

EPI realized CEO-to-worker compensation ratio (top 350 firms by sales; 2025 dollars): 20.6 (1965), 30.7 (1978), 379.6 (2000), 290.2 (2024), 324.7 (2025, projected from data through Aug 2025); realized CEO pay +1,316% vs production/nonsupervisory worker pay +28%, 1978–2025; realized pay includes exercised options and vested stock awards; ratio is an average of firm-level ratios.
